strengths: Clear formalization of what constitutes a 'good' training invariant (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness), grounding the empirical pipeline in a principled definition rather than ad hoc heuristics.

The WONDA pipeline (AST normalization + LLM-driven semantic simplification with mandatory re-verification) is a sensible, well-motivated approach to the data quality bottleneck identified in prior fine-tuning work (Wei et al., 2025), and the paper provides intuitive worked examples (Figs. 2-5) illustrating the transformation stages.

The ablation study (V0 vs V1 vs V2) convincingly isolates the contribution of normalization vs. LLM-based simplification, showing that normalization alone restores syntactic validity but LLM simplification is what drives the large gains in correctness/speedup/VBP.

The proposed VBP/VBS portfolio-based evaluation metric is a useful conceptual contribution that better reflects realistic deployment (parallel LLM + symbolic verifier) than naive sequential speedup metrics, and is a nice methodological point beyond the specific curation technique.

Consistent improvements are shown across three model scales (0.6B, 4B, 8B), and the fine-tuned 4B model achieves VBP comparable to GPT-OSS-120B, which is a meaningful demonstration that curated data can close much of the gap to much larger models at lower inference cost.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, algorithms, hyperparameters, and dataset/hardware details are provided in the appendix, and the paper states code/model/dataset release.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is small (123 hard instances) and results are averaged over only 3 runs with fairly large standard deviations (e.g., Qwen3-8B-V2 correctness 42.8±4.6%), making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for the 'Solved' timeout-resolution counts which are reported as tiny per-run integers.

All experiments rely on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) and a single benchmark source (SV-COMP/InvBench derived programs); generalization to other verifiers or program domains is left entirely to future work, limiting the demonstrated significance of the approach.

The framing that the 4B model 'approaches' GPT-5.2 undersells a fairly large remaining gap in raw correctness (44.4% vs 72.4%) and speedup rate (24.7% vs 37.1%); the VBP metric narrows this gap partly because both fail similarly often, and this nuance could be presented more critically rather than as a headline result.

The 'provable quality guarantees' language and the formal Propositions 4.1/4.3 are essentially restatements of construction-by-verification (any output that passes verifier checks is by definition correct) and add little beyond the empirical pipeline; describing this as a rigorous theoretical contribution somewhat overstates its novelty.

Key design choices (choice of Kimi K2 Thinking as the simplification LLM, N=4 candidates, verbosity threshold η) are not ablated or justified quantitatively, leaving open how sensitive the results are to these hyperparameters.

No comparison against alternative existing data-curation or filtering strategies from the literature (e.g., contrastive ranking as in iRank, or simple length/complexity filtering baselines); the only baselines are the pipeline's own intermediate stages (V0/V1) and untrained base models.

The central 'pedagogical value' / interpretability claim motivating the approach is not directly validated (e.g., via human judgment or downstream probing of whether simplified invariants actually teach transferable reasoning); the argument remains largely qualitative and illustrated only by cherry-picked examples.

No analysis of the failure/attrition rate of the LLM simplification step (e.g., what fraction of candidates are discarded for failing correctness/sufficiency checks), which would help assess the practical cost and reliability of the curation pipeline itself.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: data quality for fine-tuning LLMs on loop invariant synthesis, an area where prior work (InvBench) reported mostly negative results on hard benchmarks.

The WONDA pipeline is conceptually clean, combining a sound AST-based normalization stage with an LLM-driven semantic simplification stage that is verified post-hoc for correctness and usefulness, which is a reasonable way to avoid naive distillation pitfalls.

The paper reframes evaluation around a portfolio-based Virtual Best Performance (VBP) metric rather than naive sequential speedup, which is a sensible and arguably more realistic way to assess LLM-augmented verification in a deployment setting where the LLM runs in parallel with the symbolic baseline.

The ablation study (V0 vs V1 vs V2) is a useful internal control that isolates the contribution of normalization versus LLM-driven simplification, and shows a consistent trend across three model scales.
Reproducibility artifacts (code, data, models) are promised to be released.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is extremely small (n=123 'hard' instances, only 20 of which are baseline timeouts), and results are reported as mean ± std over only 3 runs; many of the headline comparisons (e.g., Qwen3-8B-V2 vs base, 42.8% vs 23.9% correctness) have overlapping or large relative uncertainty, and no significance testing is performed, undermining claims of 'significant' and 'consistent' gains.

The theoretical content (Proposition 4.1 Normalization Soundness, Proposition 4.3 Pipeline Soundness) is essentially trivial — AST rewrite rules preserving logical equivalence, and a filtering step that only emits verifier-approved invariants by construction — yet is advertised in the abstract as 'provable quality guarantees,' which overstates the actual technical contribution.

The LLM-based simplification stage uses another frontier model (Kimi K2 Thinking) to generate training data, which reintroduces a 'teacher' dependency the paper explicitly criticizes UAutomizer-based distillation for (the 'overfitting trap' argument in the intro); the paper does not adequately address why dependence on one strong LLM teacher is conceptually different from dependence on a symbolic teacher, nor does it quantify how much of the gain stems from Kimi's capability versus the curation methodology itself.

Comparisons against GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-5.2 are framed as the fine-tuned 4B model 'matching'/'approaching' these large models, but the absolute correctness rate gap remains large (44.4% vs 72.4% for GPT-5.2), and the 'matching' claim rests almost entirely on the VBP metric, where absolute time differences are modest (~2-20s against baselines of 165-185s) — this is a much weaker claim than the abstract conveys.

Generalization evidence is narrow: only one backend verifier (UAutomizer), one training/evaluation data source (InvBench-derived programs, largely SV-COMP), and only one base model family (Qwen3) are tested; robustness across verifiers or architectures is left to future work, limiting confidence that the curation approach generalizes.

The 'Solved' column and some reported statistics (e.g., triplets of integers for timeout resolution) are presented ambiguously without clear aggregate statistics (mean/std), making it hard to assess how reliably the approach solves genuinely hard (timeout) cases, which is the paper's central motivating use case.

For the smallest model (Qwen3-0.6B), the correctness rate is essentially unchanged after WONDA curation (28.5% base vs 27.9% curated), which is in tension with the paper's broader narrative of consistent improvement from data curation, and is not discussed with sufficient nuance beyond a post-hoc 'quality over quantity' framing.

The paper's quality grading function Q is defined relative to the UAutomizer baseline runtime on the same raw query; this conflates 'good training signal' with 'invariants that happen to be faster than one specific solver on one specific hardware configuration,' raising concerns about how transferable the resulting 'golden' dataset is to different verifiers, timeouts, or hardware.

strengths: The paper is well-grounded formally: it builds on Hoare logic to precisely define verification queries, invariant correctness/sufficiency, and a quality grading function (Definition 4.2), which gives the data curation process a principled basis rather than ad hoc heuristics.

The WONDA pipeline is a sensible two-stage design (AST-based normalization followed by LLM-driven semantic simplification with verifier-in-the-loop quality filtering) that directly targets a plausible failure mode of prior fine-tuning efforts (training on verbose, verifier-specific raw invariants).

The ablation in Table 4 convincingly isolates the contribution of each pipeline stage (V0 vs. V1 vs. V2), showing a clear, monotonic improvement in correctness and speedup rates as curation quality increases, which supports the central claim that data quality (not just fine-tuning per se) drives gains.

The proposed Virtual Best Performance (VBP)/Virtual Best Solver framing is a useful and practically motivated alternative to naive speedup metrics, correctly capturing the zero-risk portfolio deployment scenario where LLM-generated invariants run in parallel with a symbolic baseline.

The headline result -- that a 4B parameter fine-tuned SLM approaches the practical utility of GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-5.2 while avoiding reasoning-time overhead -- is a meaningful and practically relevant contribution if it holds up, since it suggests specialization can substitute for scale in this domain.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, hardware/tooling configuration, and promised release of code, data, and models.
weaknesses: The evaluation set of hard instances is quite small (n=123, with only 3 runs), and several reported metrics have large standard deviations relative to the effect sizes being claimed (e.g., Qwen3-8B base Rvalid = 89.4±7.8); this raises concerns about the statistical robustness of the comparisons, especially for the 'Solved' timeout-resolution column where differences are on the order of 1-2 instances.

No comparison against other existing learning-based or LLM-based invariant generation baselines from the related work section (e.g., LEMUR, iRank, ACInv, Loopy); the only baselines are off-the-shelf frontier LLMs and the paper's own ablations, making it hard to contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific curation method versus simply having any fine-tuning signal.

Even after curation, absolute correctness rates remain modest (22.8%-44.4%), meaning the majority of generated invariants are still not valid inductive invariants; the paper does not deeply analyze remaining failure modes or why correctness saturates around this level.

The data curation pipeline itself depends on another LLM (Kimi K2 Thinking) for the semantic simplification step, introducing a degree of circularity/dependency on a particular external model's capabilities that is not analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to choice of simplifier LLM, cost of running N=4 candidates per instance at scale).

The formal propositions (4.1 Normalization Soundness, 4.3 Pipeline Soundness) are fairly immediate consequences of the construction (verification-gated filtering trivially guarantees correctness of accepted outputs) and are presented with more formal weight than their actual technical depth warrants.

The training and evaluation data are derived entirely from a single verifier (UAutomizer) and a single benchmark source (SV-COMP via InvBench), so generalization to other verifiers or program domains is untested, a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not mitigate experimentally.

The paper's claims of 'doubling' correctness/speedup rates, while numerically accurate, should be read against the small absolute baseline values and limited sample size; the framing in the abstract could be seen as slightly overstating practical significance relative to the modest absolute performance levels achieved.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a plausible and underexplored issue (raw solver-generated invariants are structurally noisy/verbose and may not be 'learnable' targets) and formalizes desired properties of good training invariants (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness).

The WONDA pipeline is methodologically sound: AST-based normalization with simple, provably semantics-preserving rewrite rules, followed by LLM-driven simplification that is explicitly re-verified for correctness and sufficiency before being accepted as training data, ensuring the final curated dataset is sound by construction.

Thorough empirical evaluation across three model families (Qwen3 0.6B-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and multiple metrics (correctness, speedup rate, VBP, VBP_E2E), with an explicit ablation isolating the contribution of normalization (V1) versus LLM simplification (V2), showing consistent improvements from V0->V1->V2 across nearly all models and both easy/hard splits.
Good supplementary material: detailed prompts, algorithms, dataset statistics, hardware/verifier configuration, and hyperparameters are provided, supporting reproducibility.

The qualitative case study (Figure 5, cohendiv example) is a compelling illustration of how case-enumeration invariants are compressed into closed-form expressions, giving intuitive insight into why the method helps.

The comparisons against much larger off-the-shelf and frontier models (Qwen3-80B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.2) contextualize the practical value of small-model fine-tuning for a compute/cost-sensitive application.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest even after fine-tuning: correctness rates on the hard split top out around 43-45% and speedup rates around 14-25%, considerably below GPT-5.2's 72.4%/37.1%; the paper's framing (e.g., 'matches GPT-5.2') rests heavily on the aggregate VBP_E2E metric, which is dampened by the parallel virtual-best-solver fallback to the baseline verifier and can mask substantial gaps in raw model capability (Rcorrect).

The 'provable quality guarantees' and soundness propositions (4.1, 4.3) are essentially restatements that verifier checks pass by construction; they do not add substantive theoretical depth beyond the empirical pipeline design, so the framing as a rigorous formal contribution may be overstated.

Evaluation is based on relatively small samples (n=123 hard instances, 3 runs), and reported differences between many model configurations have overlapping error bars (e.g., Qwen3-14B vs Qwen3-14B-V2 correctness 36.3±1.9 vs 43.4±4.9); no formal statistical significance testing is reported, making some comparative claims less conclusive.

The 'Solved' timeout-resolution numbers are very small in absolute count (e.g., 3-4 instances per run out of 20), so claims about WONDA-trained models resolving more baseline timeouts than GPT-5.2 rest on very thin evidence.

The method depends entirely on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) for both raw invariant collection and quality grading, and timing-based grading (tv < tb) can be sensitive to machine/load noise; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not empirically test robustness to using an alternative verifier or noisier timing conditions.

No direct comparison to iterative generate-and-verify baselines (Lemur, Loopy, ACInv) that are discussed in related work; since the paper claims one-shot and iterative approaches are complementary, an empirical comparison or combination would strengthen the significance claims.

The LLM simplification step uses a large model (Kimi K2 Thinking) to generate training data for smaller models; the paper does not discuss the cost/overhead of this data-generation step or potential distillation biases introduced by relying on a single large teacher model for semantic rewriting.

Generalizability beyond C/SV-COMP style benchmarks and the specific Hoare-logic verification setting used by InvBench is untested, limiting confidence in broader applicability of the curation approach.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically important problem (loop invariant synthesis for program verification) and clearly formalizes the verification procedure (Hoare-triple based correctness/sufficiency checks, VBS/VBP metrics) in a precise and reproducible way.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: six base model families/scales (Qwen3-0.6B/4B/8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), an ablation across V0/V1/V2 curation stages, an easy/hard split, a post-hoc timeout sweep, and comparisons against strong off-the-shelf baselines (Qwen3-80B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.2).

The V0->V1->V2 ablation (Table 4) is a genuinely useful piece of evidence showing that naively fine-tuning on raw solver output can hurt validity, and that the proposed normalization+LLM-simplification stages recover and surpass baseline performance consistently across families.
Good transparency in reproducibility details: prompts, hyperparameters, hardware, UAutomizer configuration, and dataset statistics are all included in the appendix.
The qualitative examples (Figures 1, 3, 5, 6) are illustrative and help ground the abstract claims about invariant compactness and verifier speedup in concrete, interpretable cases.
weaknesses: The claimed 'provable quality guarantees' are overstated: Proposition 4.1 is a routine logical-identity argument and Proposition 4.3 is essentially a restatement of the filtering definition ('returned only if it passes the checks'), not a non-trivial theoretical contribution. This framing in the abstract/title oversells the rigor of the method.

Absolute performance remains modest: even the best fine-tuned models achieve only ~43-57% correctness and ~16-25% speedup rate on the hard split, while GPT-5.2 reaches 72.4% correctness; the headline claims ('nearly double', 'triples', 'matches frontier models') describe relative gains or a single aggregate metric (VBPE2E) that can mask this large absolute correctness gap.

The curation pipeline depends on a very strong LLM (Kimi K2 Thinking) to generate and simplify candidate invariants; this conflates 'data curation' with implicit distillation from a frontier model, which is not clearly acknowledged as a potential confound when claiming that small fine-tuned models can match/outperform large off-the-shelf models.

Statistical robustness is limited: results are averaged over only 3 runs on a hard split of 123 instances, with visibly large standard deviations in several metrics (e.g., Rcorrect, Rspeedup) that are comparable in magnitude to the reported gains between models/ablation stages; no significance testing is reported.

The pipeline is entirely dependent on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) for seed invariants, which the authors acknowledge, but this substantially limits generality and raises the question of whether gains are partly specific to UAutomizer's output style/artifacts rather than a general notion of 'high-quality' invariants.

VBP/VBPE2E assume the LLM and baseline verifier run in perfect, resource-independent parallel; in practice running an LLM (even an SLM) concurrently with a resource-intensive symbolic verifier on shared hardware could introduce contention not reflected in the reported wall-clock numbers.

No empirical comparison against iterative refinement baselines (Lemur, Loopy) that are discussed in related work as directly complementary/competing approaches; the claim that one-shot and iterative approaches are 'complementary' is asserted but not tested.

The transformation goals for LLM-based simplification (range generalization, constraint factoring, closed-form discovery, redundancy removal) are heuristic and their relative contributions are not individually ablated, making it unclear which aspects of the pipeline actually drive the reported gains versus the LLM's general capability.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: the quality (not just quantity) of training data for fine-tuning LLMs to generate loop invariants. The framing that 'not all correct invariants are equal' (correctness vs. usefulness vs. compactness) is a clear and useful conceptual contribution.

The WONDA pipeline is methodologically sound: AST-based normalization is proven semantics-preserving (Proposition 4.1), and the LLM-based simplification stage is always followed by formal re-verification (correctness + sufficiency checks), so soundness of the final curated training data is well justified (Proposition 4.3).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1, Mistral) and multiple scales (0.6B–14B), with consistent improvements from V0→V1→V2 across nearly every configuration, and a careful ablation isolating the contribution of normalization vs. LLM simplification (Table 4).

Strong headline results: small fine-tuned models (4B/8B) match or exceed much larger off-the-shelf models (Qwen3-80B, GPT-OSS-120B) and a 14B model matches GPT-5.2 on end-to-end verification time, which is a compelling practical demonstration of the value of data curation over scale.

Good reproducibility support: full prompts (Appendix B), training hyperparameters (Appendix F), grading/simplification algorithms (Appendix C), dataset statistics (Appendix D), and verifier/hardware configuration (Appendix G) are all provided, along with qualitative examples (Figures 1, 3, 5, 6) that make the pipeline's effect concrete.
Honest limitations section acknowledging dependence on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) and lack of intermediate reasoning supervision, with sensible proposed extensions.
weaknesses: The LLM-based simplification stage uses a strong teacher model (Kimi K2 Thinking) to rewrite invariants; this conflates 'data curation' with implicit knowledge distillation from a more capable LLM into the fine-tuned small models. The paper does not disentangle how much of the gain comes from curation/compactness per se versus simply imitating a stronger model's reasoning, which weakens the central claim that 'data quality, not model scale, is the bottleneck.'

Absolute performance remains modest on the hard split: correctness rates for fine-tuned models top out around 42–45%, and speedup rates around 18–25%, so while relative gains over base models are large, the practical impact on the hardest verification instances (timeouts) is still limited (only 2–4 of 20 timeouts resolved on average).

Reported results have fairly large standard deviations (e.g., ±4–8s on VBP, ±several points on correctness/speedup rates) relative to the differences being highlighted (e.g., Qwen3-14B-V2 'matching' GPT-5.2 on VBP_E2E), and no statistical significance testing is performed, making some comparative claims (especially cross-model 'matches' statements) difficult to fully substantiate.

The curated dataset is relatively small (7,284 samples derived from only 4,000 raw invariants from a single verifier on one benchmark suite), raising questions about generalization to other program classes, languages, or verifiers beyond SV-COMP/UAutomizer.

The term 'provable quality guarantees' in the abstract is somewhat strong phrasing for a pipeline whose guarantee is essentially post-hoc verifier filtering (reject unsound candidates), rather than a constructive guarantee on the simplification process itself; this could be clarified to avoid overstatement.

No analysis of the computational/API cost of running the WONDA curation pipeline itself (LLM calls for simplification, N=4 candidates per verbose invariant, plus verifier calls for grading), which is relevant for assessing the practicality/scalability of the proposed data curation approach.
